check.q: A new graduate believes her charge nurse is impaired. Who should she notify?
check.a: The next person up the chain above the charge nurse (for example, the nurse manager or house supervisor) — when the direct supervisor is the problem, escalate to the next level.

sections.heading: Recognizing and responding to impairment
sections.body:
Impairment can come from legal, illegal, prescription, or over-the-counter substances — or from extreme emotional distress, such as returning to work the day after a close family member’s death. The ANA (2015a) says any nurse who observes or suspects impairment in any health professional, nurse or non-nurse, is obligated to immediately report to a supervisor. “Suspects” matters: you do not need proof, and you should not investigate on your own by searching lockers or testing the person.

Substance-related impairment often appears as practice patterns before it appears as obvious intoxication. Many nurses with substance use disorders are skilled and well-liked, which is why colleagues tend to explain away the signs. Report the pattern; the employer and board handle evaluation. Many boards offer alternative-to-discipline programs that allow monitored treatment and return to practice — reporting is often what gets a colleague the help they need.

table.caption: Signs that suggest impairment
rows: Behavioral
Mood swings, isolation, irritability, frequent absences or tardiness, long or frequent bathroom breaks, volunteering for narcotic-heavy assignments
Physical
Slurred speech, odor of alcohol, unsteady gait, pinpoint or dilated pupils, tremors, diaphoresis, drowsiness
Practice/medication
Frequent wasting or witnessing problems, count discrepancies, high controlled-drug use compared with peers, clients reporting unrelieved pain after doses, charting errors
Emotional distress
Tearfulness, inability to concentrate, errors after a recent loss or crisis, statements of being overwhelmed

check.q: A nurse returns to work two days after her husband’s sudden death. She has made two medication errors this shift and is crying in the med room. Is this impairment?
check.a: Yes — extreme emotional distress can impair safe practice. Respond with compassion, ensure her clients are safe, and notify the supervisor immediately so she can be relieved and supported.

sections.heading: Boundaries: therapeutic relationship, crossing, and violation
sections.body:
The therapeutic relationship exists to meet the client’s needs. The nurse holds the power — access to the body, private information, medications, and privileges — so the nurse is responsible for maintaining the boundary, even if the client initiates. A boundary crossing is a brief, purposeful departure that serves the client and returns to normal (a short, relevant self-disclosure). A boundary violation serves the nurse’s needs and harms or exploits the client: romantic or sexual relationships, financial dealings, keeping secrets with a client, excessive personal disclosure, special treatment, or coercing or restraining a client to benefit the staff member. Violations must be reported to supervisors and the state board of nursing.

Boundaries also apply to the nurse’s personal life. When a friend, neighbor, or relative asks the nurse to act as their clinician or surrogate, the nurse risks blurring personal and professional roles.
sections.example: Reflect Case (Heather Adams): A 31-year-old unmarried neighbor with a history of depression has a mother with Alzheimer disease and is estranged from her only brother, who is her legal next of kin. She asks the nurse-neighbor to be her health care decision-maker so her brother will not decide for her. The nurse’s role is to be a supportive neighbor and friend, not her clinical nurse. The course position is that serving as her health care proxy creates an ethical conflict of interest for the nurse. The best recommendation is to strongly encourage her to consult an attorney to execute a durable power of attorney for health care and a living will naming a trusted friend or other non-nurse advocate.

table.caption: Where is the line?

Return focus to the client
Giving a client your personal cell number to text you after discharge

Provide unit/clinic contact; report if a colleague does this repeatedly
Dating a current client

Decline; follow facility gift policy

check.q: A client tells the nurse, “You’re the only one who understands me. Can we keep in touch after I go home?” What is the best response?
check.a: Acknowledge the relationship’s importance, explain that the nurse’s role is professional and ends at discharge, and connect the client with ongoing support resources such as outpatient follow-up or a support group.

sections.heading: Client rights violations: the William Johnson case
sections.body:
Clinical Example C: William Johnson, 53, has COPD and schizophrenia and is seen in an outpatient clinic. He tells the nurse that during his last inpatient psychiatric admission, a psychiatric technician restrained him in bed when he refused to share his cigarettes with the technician.

Rights violated: the right to control personal possessions (his cigarettes), the right to freedom from physical restraint except in an emergency, and the right to be free from abuse and coercion. The technician’s conduct is a severe boundary violation and unethical, and likely abuse. The advocacy level is both: microsocial (protecting Mr. Johnson’s safety and rights now) and macrosocial (reporting systemic abuse in the facility so other clients are protected).
steps: Listen nonjudgmentally and believe the report enough to act; thank Mr. Johnson for telling you and assess his current safety and physical and emotional state.
Document his statements objectively, in his own words, with date and time.
Report immediately to your direct supervisor/facility administration — do not decide on your own that the report is not credible because of his psychiatric diagnosis.

Ensure reports go to appropriate protective and regulatory agencies (the state protection and advocacy agency, such as Disability Rights North Carolina, and the licensing/regulatory body for the facility or technician).
Inform Mr. Johnson of his rights and of advocacy resources he can contact directly.
Follow up on outcomes and support policy changes (staff training, restraint audits) — macrosocial advocacy.

check.q: A colleague says, “He has schizophrenia; he probably imagined it.” How should the nurse respond?
check.a: A psychiatric diagnosis does not make a report less worthy of investigation; clients with mental illness are at higher risk of abuse. The nurse reports the allegation objectively and lets the designated authorities investigate.

sections.heading: Social media and HIPAA
sections.body:
Posting confidential client information — health facts, conversations, or photographs — whether intentional or nonmalicious breaches privacy laws. Removing the name does not make a post safe: a room number, a unique condition, a date, a tattoo, or a location can identify a client. “Private” groups, disappearing messages, and deleted posts are still disclosures. Consequences include discipline by the employer and by the state board of nursing, plus civil and criminal penalties (NCSBN, 2018). Nurses must also monitor colleagues and report infractions immediately.

HIPAA allows information to be shared with those who need it for treatment, payment, or operations, using the minimum necessary. Social media is never a treatment channel. The NCSBN guidance for nurses: do not post or share client images or information; do not refer to clients in disparaging ways even without identifiers; do not “friend” current or former clients; keep professional boundaries; and report breaches promptly.

No client information; follow employer policy
Photo of the unit with a client’s whiteboard visible in the background

Identifiable client information is visible

Acceptable
No client information; supports public education

check.q: A nurse sees a coworker’s story post showing a client’s X-ray with the caption “Look what we pulled out today!” The client’s name is not visible. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Recognize it as a privacy breach (the image and context can identify the client) and report it immediately to the supervisor or privacy officer per policy; do not share or comment on it.

sections.heading: Practice errors vs conduct: the Just Culture lens
sections.body:
Not every reportable event means the same thing, and not every mistake leads to discipline. Many employers and boards of nursing sort events using a Just Culture approach. The question Just Culture asks is not “What was the outcome?” but “What choice did the nurse make?” Two nurses can make the same error — one with no harm and one with serious harm — and the response should be based on the behavior, not on luck.

Just Culture sorts practice events into three behaviors. Human error is an inadvertent slip or lapse: the nurse meant to do the right thing and did not (for example, picking up the wrong vial while interrupted). The response is to console the nurse and fix the system that made the slip easy. At-risk behavior is a choice to drift from safe practice because the nurse does not recognize the risk or believes it is justified — usually a shortcut or workaround such as skipping barcode scanning “because it is faster.” The response is coaching: help the nurse see the risk, and remove the system pressures (slow scanners, short staffing) that reward the shortcut. Repeated at-risk behavior after coaching moves closer to recklessness. Reckless behavior is a conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk — the nurse knows the danger and chooses to proceed anyway. The response is disciplinary action.

Separate from these practice events are conduct issues: drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud or falsified records, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches. These are not “errors” to be coached away. They are reported to the board of nursing, not handled only by the employer, because they reflect on the nurse’s fitness to practice and the public’s safety. For substance use, many boards offer alternative-to-discipline programs that combine monitoring with treatment.

Why does this belong in an advocacy module? Because a fair system makes reporting more likely. Nurses who fear being punished for honest errors hide them, and hidden errors repeat. Advocating for clients includes reporting your own errors promptly and supporting a culture where colleagues can do the same.

table.caption: Just Culture at a glance
rows: Human error
Inadvertent slip, lapse, or mistake; the nurse did not intend the deviation
Programs a pump at 100 mL/h instead of 10 mL/h after an interruption, then reports it
Console the nurse; report through the incident system; fix the system (interruption zones, pump limits)
At-risk behavior
A chosen shortcut; risk not recognized or believed justified
Repeatedly skips barcode scanning to save time, saying “I always check the label”
Coach; remove incentives for the shortcut; monitor; repeated drift after coaching escalates
Reckless behavior
Conscious disregard of a known, substantial, unjustifiable risk
Knowingly gives a high-alert drug with no order after being told it is unsafe
Disciplinary action; may be reported to the board

steps: Ask: Did the nurse intend the action that caused the deviation? If no — human error.
Ask: Did the nurse choose a shortcut without recognizing (or while rationalizing) the risk? If yes — at-risk behavior.
Ask: Did the nurse know the risk was substantial and proceed anyway? If yes — reckless behavior.
Ask: Is this diversion, impairment, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, or a confidentiality breach? If yes — a conduct issue that goes to the board.
Match the response to the behavior (console, coach, discipline, board report), not to whether the client happened to be harmed.

check.q: A nurse gives a client’s 0900 metoprolol to the wrong client after two clients with similar names are moved into adjacent rooms. She scanned neither wristband because the scanner on that unit has been broken for a week and staff were told to “just check names.” She reports the error immediately. How would Just Culture classify this, and what should follow?
check.a: This is primarily a system-driven event: the slip itself is human error, made more likely by a broken scanner and an unsafe workaround the unit had normalized. The response is to console the nurse, assess and monitor the client who received the drug and notify the provider, complete an incident report, and fix the system (repair the scanner, flag name alerts, separate similar-name clients). It is not a conduct issue, and her prompt self-report is exactly what a Just Culture encourages.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: reporting and chain of command
sections.body:
Patterns to expect: (1) First action when a coworker appears impaired — protect clients and notify the supervisor. (2) Who to notify — the direct supervisor, or the next level when the supervisor is involved. (3) Boundary items — which nurse behavior requires intervention. (4) Social media — which post is a violation or which statement shows understanding. (5) Rights violations — which right is violated and what to do next.

Sample item: During a night shift, a nurse notices that a colleague has slurred speech, smells of alcohol, and is about to give IV morphine to a postoperative client. Which action should the nurse take first? A. Tell the colleague to go home and offer to cover her clients. B. Ask the colleague to hand over the morphine and immediately notify the charge nurse. C. Report the colleague to the state board of nursing. D. Document the observations in an incident report before the end of the shift.
steps: Read the stem: physical signs suggesting impairment; an imminent high-risk medication administration.
Identify what is asked: the FIRST action — prioritization with a safety threat.
Spot cues: “about to give IV morphine” — client harm is imminent; impairment is suspected, not proven, which is enough.
Eliminate A: sending her home is the supervisor’s decision; an impaired person may drive; and the supervisor is not informed.
Eliminate C: board reporting may follow, but it does not protect this client right now and skips the chain of command.
Eliminate D: documentation is necessary but not first; it does nothing to stop the dose.
Choose B: it prevents imminent harm (the morphine is not given) and notifies the direct supervisor immediately, who can relieve the nurse and start the reporting process.
Reusable strategy: when a colleague’s conduct threatens a client, the first action stops the harm and goes to the direct supervisor; documentation and external reporting come after.

sections.heading: Worked case: the pattern in the controlled-substance records
sections.body: Jordan, an RN on a surgical unit, notices over two weeks that a well-liked colleague, Sam, frequently signs out hydromorphone for clients whose pain scores were 2 out of 10, often asks others to cosign wastes after the fact, and takes long breaks. Two of Sam’s clients told Jordan their pain was not relieved after doses. Today Sam seems drowsy, with pinpoint pupils, and is assigned four postoperative clients.
steps: Recognize cues: practice signs (doses with low pain scores, late waste cosigning, unrelieved pain) plus physical signs (drowsiness, pinpoint pupils) suggest opioid diversion and impairment.
Analyze: clients are at risk now (unrelieved pain, unsafe care from an impaired nurse), and the pattern suggests diversion — a conduct issue, not just a single error.
Prioritize: today’s safety first — Sam’s clients need a safe nurse and pain reassessment.

Take action: privately notify the charge nurse or nurse manager immediately with specific, objective observations; refuse to cosign any waste you did not witness; reassess the clients who reported unrelieved pain and notify the provider as needed.
Generate solutions with the supervisor: the supervisor relieves Sam from client care, follows facility policy (for-cause testing, pharmacy audit), and reports to the board as required.
Evaluate: clients receive safe care and adequate analgesia; the event is documented factually; Jordan seeks support (employee assistance) for the emotional burden of reporting a friend.

check.q: Sam says, “Please don’t tell anyone; I’ll get help on my own.” What should Jordan do?
check.a: Express concern and care for Sam, but explain that client safety requires reporting, then notify the supervisor. Agreeing to secrecy would leave clients at risk and is collusion; reporting is often the path to an alternative-to-discipline program.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Board role: the North Carolina Board of Nursing (NCBON) regulates nursing under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.). The NCBON uses a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool for practice events, classifying them as human error (an inadvertent slip — console the nurse and fix the system), at-risk behavior (a drift from safe practice where risk is not recognized — coach), or reckless behavior (conscious disregard of substantial risk — discipline). Conduct issues — drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches — are reported to the Board rather than handled only by the employer. The NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for nurses with substance use disorders.

Mandatory reports outside the chain: North Carolina is a universal reporting state for child maltreatment (G.S. 7B-301): any person who suspects a juvenile (under 18) is abused, neglected, or dependent, or died from maltreatment, must report to the county DSS director. Report suspicion; do not investigate or wait for proof. Knowingly failing to report is a crime, and good-faith reporters are immune. Telling your supervisor does not replace your own legal duty. For disabled adults (G.S. 108A-102), any person with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to the county DSS director, orally or in writing, with good-faith immunity.

Multistate practice: North Carolina is a Nurse Licensure Compact state; a nurse practicing on a multistate license is accountable to the practice laws of the state where the client is located, and discipline can affect the multistate privilege.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Module 43 Advocacy study guide, p. 1 (learning outcome 43.4), pp. 2–3 (key terms: morals, boundary violations), pp. 6–7 (concept matrix: legal issues, professional behaviors; unethical/unsafe practice, impairment, social media), and pp. 8–9 (Clinical Example C, Reflect Case Heather Adams). The worked case, tables of examples, and sample item are original.

Clarifications: (1) The chain-of-command rule (direct supervisor first) applies to workplace conduct; when the nurse witnesses imminent client harm, the nurse first acts to stop the harm, then reports immediately. (2) Legally mandated external reports (suspected child maltreatment; disabled adults needing protective services) must be made to the designated agency by the person who has the suspicion; notifying a supervisor does not satisfy that duty. (3) Boundary crossing vs violation and the NCSBN social media principles were added as standard professional-practice content. (4) In the Heather Adams case, the course states that serving as her proxy is an ethical conflict for a nurse. Strictly, a nurse is not legally barred from being a health care agent for a friend in a personal capacity; the conflict is strongest when the nurse is, or could become, the person’s clinician. The exam-safe advice is the same: recommend she work with an attorney to name a trusted non-nurse agent in a durable power of attorney for health care and complete a living will. (5) The Just Culture section (human error, at-risk behavior, reckless behavior, and conduct issues reported to the board) is not in the course study guide; it was added as standard patient-safety and regulatory content because these distinctions are tested and because the NCBON uses a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool.

mnemonics.name: STOP-TELL-WRITE for unsafe colleague conduct
mnemonics.text: STOP the harm to the client, TELL your direct supervisor (next level if the supervisor is involved), WRITE objective facts (chart client care; incident report per policy). External reports follow policy and law.

mnemonics.name: Crossing vs violation: “Whose need is being met?”
mnemonics.text: Client’s need, brief, returns to professional = crossing. Nurse’s need, secret, repeated, exploitative = violation.

pearls: The duty to report covers everyone on the team, not only nurses.
Suspicion of impairment is enough to report; do not wait for proof or investigate yourself.
First report goes to your direct supervisor; escalate if the supervisor is involved or does not act.
Protect the client before anything else when harm is imminent.
Extreme grief or emotional distress can impair practice just as substances can.
Removing a name does not make a client post safe; any identifying detail is protected.
A psychiatric diagnosis never makes an abuse report less credible or less reportable.
The nurse, not the client, is responsible for maintaining professional boundaries.
redFlags: A colleague with signs of intoxication about to give medications or perform care.
Controlled-substance discrepancies, late waste cosigning, or clients reporting unrelieved pain after documented doses.
Restraint, seclusion, or threats used for punishment, coercion, or staff benefit.
A staff member keeping secrets with, dating, or exchanging money with a client.
Client photos, details, or complaints posted on social media by any staff member.
recap: State nurse practice acts and the ANA Code require nurses to intervene in and report unsafe, unethical, substandard, or unprofessional conduct.
The chain of command starts with the nurse’s direct supervisor, who provides backup and helps with reporting.
Impairment includes substances of any kind and extreme emotional distress; report suspicion immediately.
Boundary violations, such as inappropriate relationships or coercive restraint, are reported to supervisors and the board.
William Johnson’s case shows rights violations (possessions, freedom from restraint, freedom from abuse) requiring micro and macro advocacy.
Social media posts with any identifiable client information breach privacy, with employer, board, civil, and criminal consequences.
Report objectively with facts, not labels; chart client care, not the incident report.
A nurse should not blur personal and professional roles, such as by serving as a friend’s clinician or surrogate.

checks.q: A nurse sees a surgeon skip the surgical time-out despite the circulating nurse’s request. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Speak up immediately to stop the procedure until the time-out is done (client safety), and report through the chain of command — the direct supervisor or perioperative manager — with objective documentation per policy.

checks.q: A nursing student posts “Best clinical day ever! Got to see a baby born at Mercy Hospital to a 15-year-old!” What is the problem?
checks.a: It discloses client details (age, event, facility, date) that could identify the client — a privacy breach regardless of intent. The student’s instructor and the facility should be notified, and the post removed.

checks.q: A client offers the nurse $100 for “taking such good care of me.” What is the best response?
checks.a: Thank the client warmly, decline the money, and explain that the nurse cannot accept personal gifts of money; offer an appropriate alternative such as a thank-you card to the unit or a donation per facility policy.

checks.q: A charge nurse tells a staff nurse to ignore a colleague’s obvious intoxication because the unit is short-staffed. What should the staff nurse do?
checks.a: Escalate to the next level of the chain of command (nurse manager or house supervisor) immediately; short staffing never justifies allowing an impaired nurse to care for clients.

checks.q: An LPN tells the RN she held a confused client’s arms down so she could finish a dressing faster, and that “it’s fine since she has dementia.” Which concerns does this raise?
checks.a: Physical restraint without an emergency or order, possible abuse, and disregard of the client’s rights; the RN protects the client, assesses for injury, and reports to the supervisor per policy.

checks.q: A nurse’s best friend is admitted to the nurse’s unit and asks the nurse to look up her lab results. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Decline to access the record unless assigned to the friend’s care, explain privacy rules, and encourage the friend to ask her care team; consider requesting not to be assigned to her to avoid blurring roles.
